title: MLPC Retake 2024 - Complete Exam
subject: Machine Learning and Pattern Classification
description: All 43 questions from the six consecutive MLPC retake PDF exports created on July 9, 2024. Correct answers and short explanations are included. The original density-estimation and classifier dataset figures are broken in the source PDFs and are therefore noted but not embedded.

questions.question:
Consider Bayes' rule for classification: P(omega_i | x) = p(x | omega_i) P(omega_i) / p(x). Assume a classification problem with 5 fish classes, a 100-dimensional real-valued feature space, and a training set D containing 5000 fish.

Question 1: For any fish x in D, p(x) <= 1/5000.
questions.explanation: For continuous features, p(x) is a density and is not bounded by the empirical frequency 1/5000.

questions.question:
Consider Bayes' rule for classification: P(omega_i | x) = p(x | omega_i) P(omega_i) / p(x). Assume a classification problem with 5 fish classes, a 100-dimensional real-valued feature space, and a training set D containing 5000 fish.

Question 2: For any fish x in D, p(x) is a vector with 100 values.
questions.explanation: p(x) is a scalar marginal density evaluated at the 100-dimensional vector x.

questions.question:
Consider Bayes' rule for classification: P(omega_i | x) = p(x | omega_i) P(omega_i) / p(x). Assume a classification problem with 5 fish classes, a 100-dimensional real-valued feature space, and a training set D containing 5000 fish.

Question 3: For any x, sum_i p(x | omega_i) = 1.0.
questions.explanation: Class-conditional densities do not generally sum to one across classes for a fixed x.

questions.question:
Consider Bayes' rule for classification: P(omega_i | x) = p(x | omega_i) P(omega_i) / p(x). Assume a classification problem with 5 fish classes, a 100-dimensional real-valued feature space, and a training set D containing 5000 fish.

Question 4: P(omega_1 | x) is a vector with 5 entries.
questions.explanation: P(omega_1 | x) is one scalar posterior probability.

questions.question:
Consider the 5 x 5 zero-one loss function lambda for the classification problem above, learned prior and class-conditional distributions, and a Bayesian minimum-risk classifier.

Question 5: On any specific test set T, the minimum-risk classifier has exactly the same ROC-space position as a MAP classifier.
questions.explanation: With zero-one loss, minimizing conditional risk is equivalent to choosing the maximum posterior class (MAP).

questions.question:
Consider the 5 x 5 zero-one loss function lambda for the classification problem above, learned prior and class-conditional distributions, and a Bayesian minimum-risk classifier.

Question 6: sum_i sum_j lambda_ij = 1.0.
questions.explanation: A loss matrix is not required to have entries summing to one.

questions.question:
Consider the 5 x 5 zero-one loss function lambda for the classification problem above, learned prior and class-conditional distributions, and a Bayesian minimum-risk classifier.

Question 7: Multiplying every value in lambda by 5 makes it an invalid loss function.
questions.explanation: Positive scaling preserves all risk comparisons and therefore the classifier's decisions.

questions.question:
Consider a k-nearest-neighbour classifier in a d-dimensional numeric feature space, with a training set D containing N > 0 instances of two classes and Euclidean distance. Set k = N = |D|.

Question 14: The classifier will maximally overfit the training data.
questions.explanation: Using all N neighbours heavily smooths the classifier rather than maximally overfitting.

questions.question:
Consider a k-nearest-neighbour classifier in a d-dimensional numeric feature space, with a training set D containing N > 0 instances of two classes and Euclidean distance. Set k = N = |D|.

Question 15: The resulting classifier has an expected accuracy of 1/N.
questions.explanation: The prediction is driven by the overall class majority, so accuracy is not generally 1/N.

questions.question:
Consider a k-nearest-neighbour classifier in a d-dimensional numeric feature space, with a training set D containing N > 0 instances of two classes and Euclidean distance. Set k = N = |D|.

Question 16: Every training example is classified into its correct class.
questions.explanation: Minority-class training examples are generally assigned to the global majority class.

questions.question:
Consider a k-nearest-neighbour classifier in a d-dimensional numeric feature space, with a training set D containing N > 0 instances of two classes and Euclidean distance. Set k = N = |D|.

Question 17: The resubstitution estimate on D is 1.0.
questions.explanation: The resubstitution accuracy equals the proportion of the majority class, not necessarily 1.0.

questions.question:
Consider a k-nearest-neighbour classifier in a d-dimensional numeric feature space, with a training set D containing N > 0 instances of two classes and Euclidean distance. Set k = N = |D|.

Question 18: All test examples are classified into the same class.
questions.explanation: With k = N, every query uses the full training set and receives the global majority class.

questions.question:
A decision-tree learner receives a training set D and discrete features F. It randomly selects one feature, builds a one-level tree by splitting on that feature, and labels each resulting leaf with the majority class in that node.

Question 19: Combining several such trees into a random forest makes no sense because the trees rely on incompatible features.
questions.explanation: Random forests intentionally combine diverse trees built from different feature choices.

questions.question:
A decision-tree learner receives a training set D and discrete features F. It randomly selects one feature, builds a one-level tree by splitting on that feature, and labels each resulting leaf with the majority class in that node.

Question 20: The randomly chosen feature split might have information gain zero.
questions.explanation: A randomly selected feature may be independent of the class labels and yield zero information gain.

questions.question:

Question 21: Every such decision tree has training accuracy on D higher than the default accuracy.
questions.explanation: A split may fail to improve on predicting the global majority class.

questions.question:
A decision-tree learner receives a training set D and discrete features F. It randomly selects one feature, builds a one-level tree by splitting on that feature, and labels each resulting leaf with the majority class in that node.

Question 22: Every such decision tree has exactly the default accuracy on D.
questions.explanation: Some splits improve accuracy while others do not, so exact equality is not guaranteed.

questions.question:
A decision-tree learner receives a training set D and discrete features F. It randomly selects one feature, builds a one-level tree by splitting on that feature, and labels each resulting leaf with the majority class in that node.

Question 23: The resulting structure is not a decision tree.
questions.explanation: A one-level split with labelled leaves is a valid decision tree.

questions.question:
For the same two-class dataset, consider a feedforward neural network with two inputs x1 and x2, one tanh hidden unit, and one identity-activation output. Classes are encoded as 0 (white) and 1 (black), training uses squared error, and prediction is black when output > threshold tau and white otherwise. Weights are unrestricted.

Question 30: Increasing threshold tau cannot increase recall for class 0 on the training set.
questions.explanation: Raising tau predicts white more often, which can increase recall for class 0.

Classes are encoded as 0 (white) and 1 (black), training uses squared error, and prediction is black when output > threshold tau and white otherwise. Weights are unrestricted.

Question 31: The single hidden unit is unnecessary; a network without a hidden unit can learn the same function.
questions.explanation: The tanh hidden unit introduces a nonlinearity that a network without a hidden layer cannot generally reproduce.

Question 32: Setting tau to 0.0 or 1.0 makes every possible input receive the same class from any model trained this way.
questions.explanation: The identity output is unbounded, so outputs may lie below 0 or above 1.
